question: Many papers study optimal scaling laws for training compute. Has anyone analyzed optimality for inference-time compute? For instance, self-consistency samples many outputs to find the right answers. While this is effective, can't we just sample once if we have a stronger model?

ingredients.name: answer_critical_0
ingredients.criterion: The answer must affirmatively identify recent work analyzing inference-time/test-time compute scaling, contrasting with the extensively studied training-compute scaling literature [0][1].
examples: Yes, recent papers study scaling of inference-time computation, though little earlier work existed [0]
While optimal training configurations have been extensively studied, inference-time optimality was largely unexplored [1]

ingredients.name: answer_critical_1
ingredients.criterion: The answer must frame the core question: given a fixed but non-trivial inference-time compute budget, how much can an LLM improve on a challenging prompt [0]?
examples: If an LLM is allowed a fixed amount of test-time compute, how much can its performance on a hard prompt improve? [0]
Compute-optimal inference means trading off additional inference-time compute for improved performance [1]

ingredients.name: answer_critical_2
ingredients.criterion: The answer must directly address the questioner's point with an empirical counterexample: a smaller model with a better inference strategy can match or beat a larger model, e.g., Llemma-7B with novel tree search matching Llemma-34B on MATH500 using 2x fewer FLOPs, showing Pareto-optimality of small-model-plus-sophisticated-decoding [1].
examples: Llemma-7B with a novel tree search algorithm matches Llemma-34B on MATH500 with 2x less compute [1]
A smaller model with sophisticated decoding can be Pareto-optimal, so sampling once with a stronger model is not necessarily better [1]

ingredients.name: answer_critical_3
ingredients.criterion: The answer must list concrete inference strategies evaluated, such as Greedy Search, Majority Voting, Best-of-N, Weighted Voting, and tree search variants, benchmarked across model sizes and compute budgets [1].
examples: Strategies assessed included Greedy Search, Majority Voting, Best-of-N, and Weighted Voting on two tree search algorithms [1]
Majority voting (self-consistency) is one of several strategies benchmarked for computational efficiency [1]

ingredients.name: answer_critical_4
ingredients.criterion: The answer must distinguish the two primary mechanisms for scaling test-time compute: (1) searching against dense, process-based verifier reward models, and (2) adaptively updating the model's response distribution via finetuned iterative revision, noting that naive prompting for self-correction is largely ineffective [0][2].
examples: One mechanism searches against a dense process-based verifier reward model; the other updates the proposal distribution adaptively [0]
Models finetuned to iteratively revise answers sequentially condition on previous attempts; simply prompting LLMs to self-correct tends to be ineffective [2]

ingredients.name: answer_critical_5
ingredients.criterion: The answer must state that the effectiveness of test-time scaling approaches varies critically with prompt difficulty, motivating compute-optimal strategies that adaptively allocate inference-time compute per prompt for improved efficiency [0].
examples: The effectiveness of different scaling approaches varies depending on the difficulty of the prompt [0]
A compute-optimal strategy allocates test-time compute adaptively per prompt [0]

ingredients.name: valuable_0
ingredients.criterion: The answer should connect inference-time scaling to implications for LLM pretraining, i.e., the tradeoff between inference-time and pre-training compute, including the claim that optimal test-time scaling can be more effective than scaling model parameters [0].
examples: Scaling test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters [0]
These findings have implications for how one should trade off inference-time and pre-training compute [0]

ingredients.name: valuable_1
ingredients.criterion: The answer should mention budget-constrained deployment scenarios (e.g., end devices) where smaller models with better decoding are advantageous, and note generalization to any generation task with a well-defined success measure [1].
examples: Smaller models with sophisticated decoding algorithms are beneficial in budget-constrained settings such as end devices [1]
These findings could apply to any generation task with a well-defined measure of success [1]
